summary: Defines a profile of the ACE framework that lets constrained servers hand off client authentication and authorization. It uses DTLS 1.2 or later for security between entities, with raw public keys or pre-shared keys. A resource-limited server can delegate authorization management to a trusted host with more capacity.

eli5.summary: A tiny device lets a bigger helper decide who may come in, and they all talk over a private line.

questions: what is the ace dtls profile
how does a constrained device check authorization
raw public key vs pre shared key in dtls
subtitle: How a tiny device and a client use DTLS and access tokens to decide who may access what, with a bigger server doing the thinking.

tldr.problem: A resource-constrained server cannot manage who is allowed to access its resources, but it still needs to authenticate clients and enforce permissions.
tldr.mechanism: A client gets an access token and keying material from an authorization server, uploads the token to the resource server, and then sets up a DTLS channel using a raw public key or a pre-shared key bound to that token.
tldr.outcome: The constrained server delegates authorization decisions to a more capable trusted host. RFC 9202 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9430.

today: RFC 9202 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9430. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the DTLS profile of the ACE framework.

sections.title: A DTLS Profile for ACE
sections.content:
This RFC is a profile of the ACE framework (RFC 9200). A client (C) and a resource server (RS) talk CoAP over DTLS 1.2, or a later version such as DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147). The client obtains an access token bound to a proof-of-possession (PoP) key from an authorization server (AS). It proves with that key that it is authorized to use the protected resources on the RS.

The AS also gives the client and the RS the keying material needed for the DTLS session. The profile supports raw public keys (RPKs) and pre-shared keys (PSKs). Tokens are CBOR web tokens. How the RS performs token introspection with the AS is out of scope.

The ACE framework requires mutual authentication before any application data flows. DTLS provides this if both sides prove in the handshake that they can use certain keying material, and the AS helps by putting that keying material, or information about it, into the token.
sections.eli5: The tiny device does not decide who gets in. A trusted helper gives visitors a pass, and the device only checks that the pass and the secret handshake match.

sections.title: The Three Parties and the Flow
sections.content:
There are three parties: the client, the resource server and the authorization server. A client that does not know the right AS can first send an unauthorized request to the RS. The RS refuses it and replies with AS Request Creation Hints holding the AS address. The client then asks the AS's token endpoint for an access token and receives it together with Access Information.

Communication between client and AS carries confidential data, so it must be protected for confidentiality and authenticity. The client is expected to be registered at the AS beforehand.

The client then uses the token to set up a new DTLS session with the RS. If it uses an asymmetric PoP key, it MUST upload the token to the authz-info resource on the RS before the handshake. With a symmetric key it MAY do the same, or send the token in the DTLS ClientKeyExchange message instead. In every case DTLS MUST be used in a mode with replay protection.
sections.eli5: You ask the helper for a pass, the helper gives it to you, you show it at the door, and then the two of you speak over a private line.

sections.title: Raw Public Key Mode
sections.content:
In RPK mode the client sends a token request with a req_cnf object holding its raw public key or an identifier for a key the AS already knows. The AS checks that the client is associated with that key. It issues an access token that MUST be bound to the client's RPK through the cnf claim, and it returns the ace_profile parameter set to coap_dtls where required. It MUST return rs_cnf (the RS public key) unless it is certain the client already knows it.

The AS MUST protect the integrity of the token, and its confidentiality if it holds confidential data. Before the handshake the client MUST POST the token to authz-info on the RS, wait for confirmation, then use its public key in a SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure in the DTLS handshake.

An implementation of RPK mode MUST support the cipher suite TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 and MUST support curve25519. The RS MUST check that the token is still valid, that it is the intended audience, and that an authorized AS issued the token. It also MUST be able to store one token per PoP key of every authorized client.
sections.eli5: Here each side has its own unique signature. The pass says which signature belongs to the visitor, and the door only opens if the visitor can really sign that way.

sections.title: Pre-Shared Key Mode
sections.content:
In PSK mode the client MAY include in its token request an identifier for a symmetric key. The AS checks whether it refers to a key it generated earlier for this client and RS. If not, the AS MUST generate a new symmetric key and send it to the client in the cnf parameter. The RS gets the same secret in one of three ways: inside the token (the token then MUST be encrypted with a COSE_Encrypt0 structure), by deriving it from a key identifier, or by asking the AS through token introspection.

The RFC gives an example of derivation: AS and RS share a key derivation key, and the symmetric key is computed with HKDF from that key and a CBOR array holding the constant text ACE-CoAP-DTLS-key-derivation, the key length and the access token. The key identifier MUST be unique per RS.

The client follows the PSK key exchange of RFC 4279 and MUST support TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8. To say which uploaded token it wants, it puts a cnf structure with the symmetric kid into the psk_identity field. Alternatively it can send the whole token there, treated as opaque data. If the RS cannot find a valid token from the identity, it aborts the handshake with an illegal_parameter alert.
sections.eli5: Here the helper gives the visitor and the door the same secret password. The pass tells the door which password to expect, and the handshake only works if both know it.

sections.title: Resource Access
sections.content:
Once the DTLS channel exists, the client may access the resources covered by the token it uploaded. There should be only one token per client, and a newly issued token SHOULD replace an older one. The RS must check on every request that the token is still valid, and MUST remove it once it has expired.

A request is not accepted as authorized unless all of these hold: it arrived on a channel set up by this profile, the authorization information for the client is valid, the request is for this RS, the resource URI is covered, and the method is an authorized action. Otherwise the RS rejects it. It answers 4.03 (Forbidden) when the resource is not covered, and 4.05 (Method Not Allowed) when the resource is covered but the action is not. Requests with no valid token get 4.01, SHOULD include AS Request Creation Hints, and a client getting such hints SHOULD ask the AS for a new token.

Unauthorized requests SHOULD be treated as non-fatal, so the DTLS session SHOULD be kept alive until the token expires.
sections.eli5: The door checks your pass every time you ask for something. If the pass is not good for that room, you are told no, but you are not thrown out.

sections.title: Updating and Expiring Tokens
sections.content:
Permissions can change without a new handshake. The client asks the AS for a new token, naming the kid of the PoP key of its existing DTLS channel. If the AS does not recognize that key as one issued to this client, it declines with unsupported_pop_key. The client then uploads the new token to authz-info, and the RS MUST replace the authorization information for the session identified by that key. The RS may only use a new token this way if its key is the same one used in the DTLS handshake.

The RS MUST delete tokens that are no longer valid and MUST terminate a DTLS association after the last token tied to it has expired. Before terminating, it MUST send a 4.01 error for any long-running request.

The profile RECOMMENDS CoAP over DTLS between the client or RS and the AS. Other protocols that meet the framework's security requirements MAY be used, and how credentials for that link are set up is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If your permissions change, you get a new pass and show it without leaving. When the last pass runs out, the line is hung up.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The general security considerations of RFC 9200 apply. In RPK mode the AS should not issue tokens for arbitrary public keys: without a check that the client can use the matching private key, identity misbinding attacks become possible. In PSK mode security depends on the randomness of the keys and the cipher suite. Short-lived tokens and secrets give forward-secrecy properties similar to ephemeral Diffie-Hellman; for longer-lived tokens DHE cipher suites such as TLS_DHE_PSK_* or TLS_ECDHE_PSK_* should be used.

Constrained DTLS devices are open to denial of service, because a handshake creates state. Attackers could also fill the RS with intercepted valid tokens, so the RS should set a time limit after which an unused token is deleted. Session resumption lets a client skip proving possession of the PoP key again, so it should only be used with short-lived PoP keys. The RS should avoid multiple tokens per client, and an attacker delaying or reordering packets to authz-info can make the order of updates uncertain.

On privacy, an unprotected response to an unauthorized request may reveal information about the RS or its relationship with the client, so it should contain as little as possible. Clients SHOULD NOT send confidential data in unprotected requests, and message sizes and addresses can still leak after the session is set up.
sections.eli5: Passes must be handed out only to the person they belong to, kept short-lived, and not piled up. Even a private line can show how big the messages are and who is talking.
